what: Dependent-substream decoding across every eight-channel E-AC-3 track in the library
method: Ten seconds from ten minutes into each title, so the window carries content: the first minutes of a film are often digital silence and two decoders' dither is not a measurement. Each head is decoded by oadec in the stream's own channel order and by FFmpeg with -drc_scale 0, and every oadec channel is compared against every FFmpeg channel. A channel counts as matched when the FFmpeg channel it is supposed to be beats every other by at least 10 dB, narrow when it wins by less, silent when the reference channel is at or below -80 dBFS, and mismatched when some other channel fits better.

titles.title: Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade (1989).mkv
Star Wars Episode VI Return of the Jedi (1983).mkv

reading: All 40 titles decode to eight channels and FFmpeg agrees on the count for every one.

Two custom channel maps occur in the wild: 0x1a00 on 35 titles, which names Ls, Rs and the Lrs/Rrs pair and gives 7.1, and 0xa010 on 5 titles, which names L, R and the Vhl/Vhr pair and gives 5.1.2. FFmpeg reports the same two layouts, 7.1 and 5.1.2, on the same titles.
Of 320 channel comparisons, 271 matched, 5 were narrow, 44 were silent and none was mismatched. Every title had every channel in the right place.

The five narrow cases are content, not placement: Jurassic Park's two height channels carry nearly the same signal, so the intended pairing wins by 7.85 dB rather than by a wide margin; Vertigo's surrounds sit between -66 and -76 dBFS, close enough to the dither floor that most of what is compared is the two decoders' noise. In both the intended pairing still wins.
A 5.1.2 track advertised as 7.1 in its file name is a reminder that the channel map, not the title, says what a dependent substream carries.
